c: Riverside Rockets, a minor league baseball team with a 6,000-seat stadium
s: The Riverside Rockets averaged 2,400 fans per home game last season, well below the stadium's capacity. The general manager wants to raise average attendance to 3,200 next season. The team can spend $20,000 on promotions and is considering a family-night series, a student discount with local colleges, and a giveaway night each month.
The general manager (judge) wants to know which promotions will fill seats without lowering revenue too far, and how to measure the results.
You have 7 minutes to explain the situation, compare the promotions with pros and cons, and recommend a plan.
f: Home games: 66; average attendance: 2,400; average ticket $12; average concession spending $9 per fan
Goal: 3,200 fans per game (800 more)
Family night: $5 tickets for kids, estimated cost $4,500 for six nights
Student discount: $6 tickets with ID, estimated cost $3,000
Giveaway nights: bobbleheads or caps for the first 1,000 fans, about $2,700 each time
n: Explains why promotions can fill seats and raise concession revenue
Calculates revenue effects, including the $9 concession spending per added fan
Compares family nights, student discounts and giveaways with costs and benefits
Recommends a mix that fits $20,000
Considers weather, schedule and competition from other entertainment
Sets measures such as attendance, concession revenue and promotion cost per added fan
q: If kids pay $5 and parents spend on food, does that still make money?
Which night of the week would you target and why?
How will you know a giveaway brought in new fans instead of the same fans?

c: Metro City Marathon, an annual charity race with 4,000 runners
s: The Metro City Marathon is eight weeks away and the race director is worried about several issues: registrations are 600 short of last year, two course sections need rerouting for road work, and the main sponsor has pulled out, leaving a $30,000 gap in the budget.

The race director (judge) wants a plan that keeps the race on schedule and financially sound. The options include shortening the course, finding replacement sponsors, raising registration fees, or reducing event services. Each affects runners, sponsors and the charity beneficiary.
You have 7 minutes to present your plan with the alternatives and pros and cons.
f: Registrations: 3,400 (goal 4,000); fee $65 per runner
Missing sponsor funds: $30,000
Course issue: two miles need rerouting; permits take 3 to 4 weeks
Charity beneficiary expects at least $60,000 in donations
Costs cut if services are reduced: about $14,000
n: Prioritizes problems by deadline and impact
Compares fee increases, new sponsors, reduced services and course changes with pros and cons
Recommends a combined plan that closes the $30,000 gap
Includes the permit timeline for rerouting
Communicates with runners, sponsors and the public
Sets measures such as registrations by week and funds raised
q: Would raising the fee hurt registrations?
How do you keep the charity beneficiary on board?
What would you cut first if you can't find a sponsor?

c: Summit City Thunder, a professional basketball team
s: A video of a Thunder player arguing with a fan during a game has spread on social media and been picked up by a local news station. The fan says the player used insulting language. The team is still gathering facts, but sponsors are asking questions and ticket sales dropped 8 percent this week.

The team president (judge) wants a public relations plan right away. The options include issuing a quick statement, waiting until an investigation is finished, suspending the player, or holding a press conference with the player. The team's reputation, sponsors, fans and the player are all affected.
You have 7 minutes to explain your plan, compare options with pros and cons, and recommend a response.
f: Video views: 1.2 million in 48 hours
Ticket sales down 8% this week; two sponsors have asked for a call
Player is a team leader and a fan favorite
The investigation is expected to take 5 days
The team has a community program that reaches 12,000 students
n: Recommends acting quickly with a short, honest statement while saying an investigation is underway
Compares a statement, suspension, press conference and silence with pros and cons
Identifies audiences: fans, sponsors, the media, the player and the fan involved
Plans separate messages and a spokesperson
Protects the team's long-term reputation, using its community program
Sets measures such as sentiment, sponsor retention and ticket sales
q: What if the facts come out and the player was in the wrong?
What do you say to the sponsors who called?

c: Harbor City Symphony, an orchestra that performs 40 concerts a season
s: The Harbor City Symphony's concert hall has 1,200 seats, but only 58 percent are sold on average. Subscribers are aging, and the executive director wants to attract younger audiences without losing the revenue that loyal subscribers provide, because an empty seat earns nothing but a seat sold cheaply still adds a little. Ideas include dynamic pricing, a $15 under-30 ticket, and a pay-what-you-can night.
The executive director (judge) wants you to analyze pricing and recommend changes for next season.

The orchestra has tried discounts before, but only as one-time emails, and never measured whether they brought in new patrons or simply gave regular patrons a cheaper night. You have 7 minutes to present your analysis and recommendation.
f: Seats: 1,200; average sold: 696 (58%); average ticket price $48
Subscribers: 280 seats per concert at a 15% discount
Under-30 ticket idea: $15 for unsold seats, limited to 150 per concert
Dynamic pricing could raise the price of high-demand dates by 15% and lower low-demand dates by 20%
Costs per concert: about $41,000
n: Calculates current revenue per concert (about $33,400) against costs
Compares under-30 tickets, dynamic pricing and pay-what-you-can, with pros and cons
Explains how unsold seats have zero extra cost and why selling them cheaply may help
Estimates the effect of 150 added young attendees at $15 ($2,250 per concert)
Considers the effect on full-price buyers
Recommends a plan and a way to measure sales by age group
q: Won't regular customers just wait for the cheap tickets?
Why not simply lower prices for everyone?
How will you reach people under 30?

c: Summit Climbing Gym, a new indoor climbing gym
s: Summit Climbing Gym opened four months ago with a goal of 600 members, but has only 310. The owner has an advertising budget of $6,000 for the next three months and wants to know how to use it. The gym is in a city with two universities and a large number of young professionals.
The owner (judge) is considering local social media ads, a partnership with the universities' outdoor clubs, radio spots and a free first-visit offer.
You have 7 minutes to explain the audience, compare the advertising choices with pros and cons, and recommend a campaign.
f: Members: 310 (goal 600); monthly fee $62
Budget: $6,000 over three months
Social ads: about $1,800 for a 6-week campaign; radio: $3,500 for 40 spots; club partnerships: $800 plus staff time
Free first visit would cost about $14 in staff and equipment per person
Survey of members: 54% found the gym through friends or Instagram
n: Defines the target audience from the survey and the local market
Compares media options on reach, cost and fit
Recommends a plan within $6,000 that favors social media and partnerships over radio
Includes a message and an offer
Sets goals, such as 120 new members
Explains how to track which ads bring in members
q: Why not spend most of the budget on radio?
How will you know an ad worked?
What would you say in a 15-second video?
